Then the system's own way of making a mess could change from run to run.

[L72] PREFATORY NOTE
[L73] The editor has not attempted to give within the limits of this single volume a detailed history of the development of both pianoforte and chamber music. He has emphasized but very little the historical development of either branch of music, and he has not pretended to discuss exhaustively all the music which might be comprehended under the two broad titles.

[L75] The chapters on pianoforte music are intended to show how the great masters adapted themselves to the exigencies of the instrument, and in what manner they furthered the development of the difficult technique of writing for it. Also, because the piano may be successfully treated in various ways, and because it lends itself to the expression of widely diverse moods, there is in these chapters some discussion of the great masterpieces of pianoforte literature in detail.

[L77] The arrangement of material is perhaps not usual. What little has been said about the development of the piano, for example, has been said in connection with Beethoven, who was the first to avail himself fully of the advantages the piano offered over the harpsichord. A discussion, or rather an analysis, of the pianoforte style has been put in the chapter on Chopin, who is even today the one outstanding master of it.

[L79] In the part of the book dealing with chamber music the material has been somewhat arbitrarily arranged according to combinations of instruments. The string quartets, the pianoforte trios, quartets, and quintets, the sonatas for violin and piano, and other combinations have been treated separately. The selection of some works for a more or less detailed discussion, and the omission of even the mention of others, will undoubtedly seem unjustifiable to some; but the editor trusts at least that those he has chosen for discussion may illumine somewhat the general progress of chamber music from the time of Haydn to the present day.

[L81] For the chapters on violin music before Corelli and the beginnings of chamber music we are indebted to Mr. Edward Kilenyi, whose initials appear at the end of these chapters.

[L86] INTRODUCTION
[L87] The term Chamber Music, in its modern sense, cannot perhaps be strictly defined. In general it is music which is fine rather than broad, or in which, at any rate, there is a wealth of detail which can be followed and appreciated only in a relatively small room. It is not, on the whole, brilliantly colored like orchestral music. The string quartet, for example, is conspicuously monochrome. Nor is chamber music associated with the drama, with ritual, pageantry, or display, as are the opera and the mass. It is—to use a well worn term—very nearly always absolute music, and, as such, must be not only perfect in detail, but beautiful in proportion and line, if it is to be effective.

[L89] As far as externals are concerned, chamber music is made up of music for a solo instrument, with or without accompaniment (excluding, of course, concertos and other like forms, which require the orchestra, and music for the organ, which can hardly be dissociated from cathedrals and other large places), and music for small groups of instruments, such as the string trio and the string quartet, and combinations of diverse instruments with the piano. Many songs, too, sound best in intimate surroundings; but one thinks of them as in a class by themselves, not as a part of the literature of chamber music.

[L91] With very few exceptions, all the great composers have sought expression in chamber music at one time or another; and their compositions in this branch seem often to be the finest and the most intimate presentation of their genius. Haydn is commonly supposed to have found himself first in his string quartets. Mozart’s great quartets are almost unique among his compositions as an expression of his genius absolutely uninfluenced by external circumstances and occasion. None of Beethoven’s music is more profound nor more personal than his last quartets. Even among the works of the later composers, who might well have been seduced altogether away from these fine and exacting forms by the intoxicating glory of the orchestra, one finds chamber music of a rich and special value.

[L93] This special value consists in part in the refined and unfailing musical skill with which the composers have handled their slender material; but more in the quality of the music itself. The great works of chamber music, no matter how profound, speak in the language of intimacy. They show no signs of the need to impress or overwhelm an audience. Perhaps no truly great music does. But operas and even symphonies must be written with more or less consideration for external circumstances, whereas in the smaller forms, composers seem to be concerned only with the musical inspiration which they feel the desire to express. They speak to an audience of understanding friends, as it were, before whom they may reveal themselves without thought of the effectiveness of their speech. They seem in them to have consulted only their ideals. They have taken for granted the sympathetic attention of their audience.

[L95] The piano has always played a commanding rôle in the history of chamber music. From the early days when the harpsichord with its figured bass was the foundation for almost all music, both vocal and instrumental, few forms in chamber music have developed independently of it, or of the piano, its successor. The string quartet and a few combinations of wind instruments offer the only conspicuous exceptions. The mass of chamber music is made up of pianoforte trios, quartets, and quintets, of sonatas for pianoforte and various other instruments; and, indeed, the great part of pianoforte music is essentially chamber music.

[L97] It may perhaps seem strange to characterize as remarkably fine and intimate the music which has been written for an instrument often stigmatized as essentially unmusical. But the piano has attracted nearly all the great composers, many of whom were excellent pianists; and the music which they have written for it is indisputably of the highest and most lasting worth. There are many pianoforte sonatas which are all but symphonies, not only in breadth of form, but in depth of meaning. Some composers, notably Beethoven and Liszt, demanded of the piano the power of the orchestra. Yet on the whole the mass of pianoforte music remains chamber music.

[L99] The pianoforte style is an intricate style, and to be effective must be perfectly finished. The instrument sounds at its best in a small hall. In a large one its worst characteristics are likely to come all too clearly to the surface. And though it is in many ways the most powerful of all the instruments, truly beautiful playing does not call upon its limits of sound, but makes it a medium of fine and delicately shaded musical thought. To regard it as an instrument suited primarily to big and grandiose effects is grievously to misunderstand it, and is likely, furthermore, to make one overlook the possibilities of tone color which, though often denied it, it none the less possesses.

[L101] In order to study intelligently the mechanics, or, if you will, the art of touch upon the piano, and in order to comprehend the variety of tone-color which can be produced from it, one must recognize at the outset the fact that the piano is an instrument of percussion. Its sounds result from the blows of hammers upon taut metal strings. With the musical sound given out by these vibrating strings must inevitably be mixed the dull and unmusical sound of the blow that set them vibrating. The trained ear will detect not only the thud of the hammer against the string, but that of the finger against the key, and that of the key itself upon its base. The study of touch and tone upon the piano is the study of the combination and the control of these two elements of sound, the one musical, the other unmusical.

[L103] The pianist can acquire but relatively little control over the musical sounds of his instrument. He can make them soft and loud, but he cannot, as the violinist can, make a single tone grow from soft to loud and die away to soft again. The violinist or the singer both makes and controls tone, the one by his bow, the other by his breath; the pianist, in comparison with them, but makes tone. Having caused a string to vibrate by striking it through a key, he cannot even sustain these vibrations. They begin at once to weaken; the sound at once grows fainter. Therefore he has to make his effects with a volume of sounds which has been aptly said to be ever vanishing.

[L105] On the other hand, these sounds have more endurance than those of the xylophone, for example; and in their brief span of failing life the skillful pianist may work somewhat upon them according to his will. He may cut them exceedingly short by allowing the dampers to fall instantaneously upon the strings, thus stopping all vibrations. He may even prolong a few sounds, a chord let us say, by using the sustaining pedal. This lifts the dampers from all the strings, so that all vibrate in sympathy with the tones of the chord and reënforce them, so to speak. This may be done either at the moment the notes of the chord are struck, or considerably later, after they have begun appreciably to weaken. In the latter case the ear can detect the actual reënforcement of the failing sounds.

[L107] Moreover, the use of the pedal serves to affect somewhat the color of the sounds of the instrument. All differences in timbre depend on overtones; and if the pianist lifts all dampers from the strings by the pedals, he will hear the natural overtones of his chord brought into prominence by means of the sympathetic vibrations of other strings he has not struck. He can easily produce a mass of sound which strongly suggests the organ, in the tone color of which the shades of overtones are markably evident.

[L109] The study of such effects will lead him beyond the use of the pedal into some of the niceties of pianoforte touch. He will find himself able to suppress some overtones and bring out others by emphasizing a note here and there in a chord of many notes, especially in an arpeggio, and by slighting others. Such an emphasis, it is true, may give to a series of chords an internal polyphonic significance; but if not made too prominent, will tend rather to color the general sound than to make an effect of distinct drawing.

[L111] It will be observed that in the matter of so handling the volume of musical sound, prolonging it and slightly coloring it by the use of the pedal or by skillful emphasis of touch, the pianist’s attention is directed ever to the after-sounds, so to speak, of his instrument. He is interested, not in the sharp, clear beginning of the sound, but in what follows it. He finds in the very deficiencies of the instrument possibilities of great musical beauty. It is hardly too much to say, then, that the secret of a beautiful or sympathetic touch, which has long been considered to be hidden in the method of striking the keys, may be found quite as much in the treatment of sounds after the keys have been struck. It is a mystery which can by no means be wholly solved by a muscular training of the hands; for a great part of such training is concerned only with the actual striking of the keys.

[L113] We have already said that striking the keys must produce more or less unmusical sounds. These sounds are not without great value. They emphasize rhythm, for example, and by virtue of them the piano is second to no instrument in effects of pronounced, stimulating rhythm. The pianist wields in this regard almost the power of the drummer to stir men to frenzy, a power which is by no means to be despised. In martial music and in other kinds of vigorous music the piano is almost without shortcomings. But inasmuch as a great part of pianoforte music is not in this vigorous vein, but rather in a vein of softer, more imaginative beauty, the pianist must constantly study how to subject these unmusical sounds to the after-sounds which follow them. In this study he will come upon the secret of the legato style of playing.

[L115] If the violinist wishes to play a phrase in a smooth legato style, he does not use a new stroke of his bow for each note. If he did so, he would virtually be attacking the separate notes, consequently emphasizing them, and punctuating each from the other. Fortunately for him, he need not do so; but the pianist cannot do otherwise. Each note he plays must be struck from the strings of his instrument by a hammer. He can only approximate a legato style—by concealing, in one way or another, the sounds which accompany this blow.

[L117] The so-called legato touch on the keyboard is one in which the fingers cling closely to the keys, and by which, therefore, the keys are pressed down rather than struck. In this way the player actually eliminates one of the three sounds of attack, namely, that of the finger hitting the key. To a certain extent he also minimizes the sound of the key hitting its base, a sound which, moreover, the felt cushion of the base does much to lessen. At the risk of throwing all preconceived theories of legato touch into question, it may be said that this unpleasant sound can be wholly eliminated by a sort of light, quick, lifting touch, which, without driving the key down even to its base, will yet cause the hammer to spring up and hit the string above it.

[L119] By such means as these the pianist can at least subdue, if he cannot silence, the noises which in some measure must inevitably accompany his playing. The more he can do so, the smoother and pleasanter his playing will become. In so far as the tone of the pianoforte can be sensuous

[L48] SUMMARY
[L49] Ensuring data integrity is critical in modern data-intensive science, motivating the development of scalable 
[L50] methods for anomaly detection across datasets. Benford’s law, which describes a characteristic distribution 
[L51] of leading digits in naturally occurring data, offers a domain-agnostic signal of irregularities, but its practical 
[L52] use is limited by difficulties in quantifying adherence and uncertainty, especially for datasets of varying sizes. 
[L53] We introduce simulation-based Benfordness estimation (SBBE), a Bayesian framework that models data as a 
[L54] mixture of Benford-conforming and non-conforming components. SBBE provides uncertainty-aware esti￾mates, supports interpretability, and enables principled comparisons across datasets. We validate the 
[L55] approach using simulations and real-world Benford-compliant data and apply it to bioactivity datasets, 
[L56] where it revealed irregularities and sources of deviation. These results demonstrate the value of SBBE as 
[L57] a practical proxy for assessing data quality across scientific domains.
[L58] THE BIGGER PICTURE Trusted, high-quality data are fundamental to modern scientific research, yet assess￾ing data quality remains a challenging and only partially solved problem. Most automated approaches 
[L59] depend on prior knowledge of the specific types of errors or inconsistencies to be detected. In contrast, 
[L60] one domain-independent indicator requires no such assumptions: Benford’s law, the characteristic distribu￾tion of first significant digits observed in many naturally occurring datasets. According to Benford’s law, 
[L61] numbers beginning with the digit ‘‘1’’ occur more frequently than those beginning with ‘‘2’’, which in turn 
[L62] occur more frequently than those beginning with ‘‘3’’, and so on. Deviations from this pattern can indicate 
[L63] unusual aspects of how data were generated, reported, recorded, or curated. However, existing measures 
[L64] of Benford conformity often perform poorly on large datasets and yield scores that cannot be compared 
[L65] directly across datasets of different sizes. 
[L66] We introduce simulation-based Benfordness estimation (SBBE), a method that estimates the proportion of a 
[L67] dataset that conforms to Benford’s law. SBBE provides uncertainty estimates and produces scores that are 
[L68] directly comparable across datasets regardless of size. Applied to bioactivity data, SBBE ranks databases in 
[L69] accordance with their curation standards and prioritizes a small subset of assay datasets for expert review. 
[L70] Examination of these prioritized datasets revealed diverse sources of irregularity, ranging from reporting 
[L71] practices, such as rounding measurements on a logarithmic scale, to genuine curation errors, including 
[L72] the collapse of value ranges (e.g., 100–1,000) into a single reported value. Because SBBE relies solely on 
[L73] the numerical values themselves, it is inherently domain agnostic and offers a rapid, versatile approach for 
[L74] detecting data irregularities across scientific disciplines.

[L81] INTRODUCTION
[L82] Data are the cornerstone of modern research, but their true value 
[L83] depends on their integrity. Even minor errors can have major con￾sequences. The failure of the Mars Climate Orbiter, for instance, 
[L84] was traced back to a simple mismatch in measurement units.1
[L85] Similarly, inconsistencies within or across databases can under￾mine the integrity of scientific findings.2–5 In historical hurricane￾tracking databases, such inconsistencies led to decades of under￾counted storms, complicating assessment of climate models.6
[L86] Ensuring data quality requires vigilance at multiple levels, from 
[L87] the accuracy of individual samples7 to the harmonization and 
[L88] validation of entire dataset collections.3,4 While small numbers 
[L89] of data samples can be checked manually, such approaches 
[L90] are infeasible at scale.
[L91] Today, computational methods are widely employed to detect 
[L92] data irregularities that may reflect errors, rare events, or unex￾pected patterns.8–10 Common approaches include data clus￾tering to identify outliers,8,11,12 comparison with historical data 
[L93] to reveal temporal shifts,9 and isolation forests that flag data￾points easily separable from the bulk of the data.13 Building on 
[L94] these foundations, more advanced techniques extend irregular￾ity detection to the dataset level. For example, summary statis￾tics or learned features from meta-learning enable clustering of 
[L95] datasets,14 while active learning refines noisy labels by selecting 
[L96] ambiguous cases for expert review.15 Yet, these approaches 
[L97] intensify the curse of dimensionality, as each dataset aggregates 
[L98] already high-dimensional samples, complicating both detection 
[L99] and interpretation.16 This highlights a critical gap: the lack of 
[L100] scalable, domain-agnostic heuristics to flag irregularities at the 
[L101] dataset level.
[L102] An underexplored yet promising approach for uncovering hid￾den irregularities in datasets is Benford’s law.17,18 This mathe￾matical principle posits that in naturally occurring datasets, 
[L103] smaller digits are more likely to appear as leading digits. For 
[L104] example, numbers beginning with ‘‘1’’ occur more frequently 
[L105] than those starting with ‘‘2’’, which in turn are more common 
[L106] than those starting with ‘‘3’’, and so forth.17,18
[L107] Data from a wide range of domains have been found to follow 
[L108] Benford’s law, particularly when values span several orders of 
[L109] magnitude. Because this pattern appears so consistently, Ben￾ford’s law has been employed to flag irregularities such as 
[L110] data noise, anomalies, or even potential fraud. In finance, it sup￾ports auditing by identifying suspicious patterns in transaction 
[L111] records.19 In public health, it was used during the COVID-19 
[L112] pandemic to assess the reliability of reported infection rates, 
[L113] revealing potential data manipulation.20,21
[L114] More recently, Benford’s law has shown promise for flagging 
[L115] data generated by artificial intelligence (AI) systems. Several 
[L116] studies22–24 employed Benford’s law to distinguish AI-generated 
[L117] from human-written text. In the image domain, Zago et al.25 re￾ported that images generated by adversarial neural networks 
[L118] deviate from Benford’s law relative to natural images. Beyond 
[L119] text and images, Bantange et al.26 used Benford’s law to analyze 
[L120] the distribution of musical note frequencies. They were able to 
[L121] distinguish human-composed music (e.g., by Johann Sebastian 
[L122] Bach) from AI-generated music that emulates Bach’s style.
[L123] Importantly, deviations from Benford’s law should not be 
[L124] viewed as evidence of data manipulation by default. Routine 
[L125] methodological factors can readily shift the observed first-digit 
[L126] frequencies away from the Benford distribution. These include 
[L127] rounding practices, binning strategies, and limited dynamic 
[L128] ranges, all of which are common in scientific measurement pipe￾lines and can produce systematic distortions.27 Yet, deviations 
[L129] can also be informative: in geophysics, the low signal-to-noise 
[L130] characteristics of marsquake recordings introduce departures 
[L131] from Benford’s pattern that can be exploited for event detec￾tion.28 Thus, interpreting Benford irregularities requires distin￾guishing artifacts of data processing from domain-specific signal 
[L132] features.
[L133] A variety of methods exist for quantifying a dataset’s confor￾mity with Benford’s law (‘‘Benfordness,’’ see the ‘‘terminology’’ 
[L134] subsection of the methods section). These include classical 
[L135] goodness-of-fit (frequentist) tests, such as the chi-squared 
[L136] test,29,30 and Bayesian model comparison measures, such as 
[L137] the Bayes factor (BF)31 (supplemental methods). The chi￾squared test compares the observed and expected (Benford) 
[L138] first significant digit (FSD) frequencies by calculating the squared 
[L139] differences between them. The BF, on the other hand, measures 
[L140] how strongly the data support a Benford model relative to an 
[L141] alternative model.
[L142] Although grounded in different statistical frameworks, both fre￾quentist tests and Bayesian approaches exhibit similar limitations 
[L143] when used to assess conformity to Benford’s law. Both are sensi￾tive to sample size and tend to produce inflated results for large 
[L144] datasets, even with minor deviations.30 Moreover, both ap￾proaches yield single-number outputs (chi-squared test and BF) 
[L145] that are not directly comparable across datasets of different sizes.
[L146] For the chi-squared test, one approach to rescale the test sta￾tistic is to use relative frequencies (proportions) rather than abso￾lute frequencies (raw counts).29,32,33 However, this violates the 
[L147] assumptions of the statistical test and can produce misleading 
[L148] results.30,34
[L149] Beyond generic goodness-of-fit methods, Leemis35 formal￾ized a Benford-specific statistic assessing adherence to Ben￾ford’s law based on the most deviant FSD proportion. This 
[L150] made discrepancies easy to localize and explain (e.g., too 
[L151] many 5s as an FSD). Morrow36 built on this by adding a sam￾ple-size-based scaling factor to improve small-sample reliability. 
[L152] However, these methods still yield a single value and may flag 
[L153] large datasets based on minor deviations.
[L154] To evaluate the different Benfordness measures, studies typi￾cally use Monte Carlo simulations.37 Under a specified data￾generating model, repeated samples are drawn, and the statistic 
[L155] of interest is computed. Because the generating model is known, 
[L156] the strengths and weaknesses of Benfordness measures can be 
[L157] quantified. Typically, a common setup considers mixtures of 
[L158] Benford and uniform FSD distributions, where the uniform 
[L159] component proportion is interpreted as contamination.37,38
[L160] Similarly, in practice, data often originate from multiple sour￾ces, such as different laboratories or different databases. 
[L161] Consider a dataset composed of two underlying sources: one 
[L162] that follows Benford’s law and one that does not. If it were known 
[L163] how much of a dataset comes from a source following Benford’s 
[L164] law and how much comes from a source that does not, the Ben￾fordness of a dataset (i.e., one minus the contamination or, in 
[L165] other words, the data sample’s proportion coming from Ben￾ford’s FSD distribution) could be quantified directly.

Experimental microtonal pop colliding with industrial dub, Balkan brass, and broken algorithmic folk. 137 BPM, with a drifting 5/8 pulse that intermittently snaps into straight 4/4 and then loses its downbeat. Close-miked female vocals, alternating between clinical spoken delivery, unnaturally sustained vowels, and short, compulsively repeated phrases. Detuned accordion, dry darbuka, bowed metallic strings, sub-bass pulses, and tiny granular vocal fragments. Technical phrases remain intelligible until repetition gradually deforms their stress patterns. Abrupt gaps, clipped consonants, phrases restarting mid-word, and brief sections where the percussion follows a different tempo from the voice. Narrow, intimate mono recording with tape flutter, occasional extreme stereo expansion, and deliberately exposed edits. The emotional tone shifts between bureaucratic neutrality, inexplicable tenderness, and mechanical insistence. No conventional chorus resolution. Let repetitions mutate unevenly; preserve any accidental rhythmic or phonetic patterns that emerge. Avoid smoothing the contradictions into a coherent narrative.

parts: Creativity is in curating. And making room for the unexpected.

Yes. Curation is the art; the machinery is there to make things happen that you couldn't have planned.

The source dump is a field of possibilities. You choose what enters the room, but not necessarily what happens once it’s there. A technical phrase survives the shredder. A footnote collides with a rhythm. Something apparently irrelevant becomes the hinge. Something *important* gets thrown away.

The script shouldn't try to make everything cohere. It should generate more accidents than it can explain, then give you interesting things to keep, cut, or mutate again.

**Not randomness instead of taste. Randomness in service of taste.**

And the crucial bit: curation shouldn't just clean up the mess. It should sometimes recognize the mess as the thing.
